explanation: Early IOP elevation after an open-globe or other penetrating injury is usually mechanical: red blood cells, fibrin and their breakdown products obstruct the trabecular meshwork after a traumatic hyphema, so blood in the anterior chamber is by far the commonest cause. Traumatic iritis is near universal but inflammation more often lowers IOP by suppressing aqueous secretion, and it raises pressure only when trabeculitis, synechiae or lens material are added. Fibrous ingrowth, like the related epithelial downgrowth, is a rare late complication of a penetrating wound or surgical incision; it is a classic cause of intractable secondary glaucoma but is far too uncommon to be the most frequent cause of raised IOP after trauma.
concern: I disagree with the key on frequency grounds. The recall is ambiguous about timing: if the examiner meant late, refractory secondary glaucoma months after a penetrating wound, fibrous ingrowth becomes defensible, but for IOP rise after penetrating trauma in general, hyphema dominates. Note also that the source explanation describes epithelial downgrowth after intraocular surgery, which is not one of the offered options, so the key is not supported by its own text.

explanation: A fragment that will not travel to the phaco tip is a followability problem, and distal followability, meaning how readily material is attracted to the aspiration port, is improved by raising the aspiration flow rate; proximal followability, meaning how well material is held at the port, is improved by raising vacuum. Lowering the flow rate would make the reluctant fragment even less likely to come to the tip. Burst mode alters only how ultrasound energy is delivered and tends to repel fragments (chatter) rather than attract them, and raising vacuum without flow mainly improves holding once occlusion has occurred.
concern: The source key (decrease aspiration flow rate) directly contradicts the source's own quoted explanation, which states that distal followability is improved by increasing the aspiration flow rate. The one argument for lowering flow is the second half of the stem, small fragments moving rapidly in the chamber, which suggests excessive turbulence and surge; if the examiner's emphasis was chamber instability rather than followability, reducing flow or raising the bottle would be reasonable. The item as recalled describes both problems at once and is internally conflicted, hence medium confidence.

explanation: Wound burn is a thermal injury that occurs when irrigation fluid can no longer flow around the phaco needle to carry away the heat generated by ultrasound. The commonest cause is an incision that is too tight, compressing the silicone sleeve against the needle and choking off that cooling flow; occlusion of the aspiration line by dense nuclear material or retained viscoelastic produces the same result. Increasing the infusion rate would if anything cool the wound better, and vacuum alone generates no heat, so neither of those options is the mechanism.

With affected father and grandfather she has hereditary retinoblastoma, so she carries one mutant RB1 allele and transmits it to each child with probability 0.5, independently for every pregnancy. Multiplying by the stated penetrance of 0.8 gives a 0.4 risk that any individual child, including the first, actually develops a tumour. Option C (0.5) is the chance of inheriting the gene rather than of expressing disease, option D multiplies the two figures a second time, and 0.1 corresponds to nothing in this pedigree. Note that her husband's negative family history is irrelevant because the trait is dominant.

Multiple facial neurofibromas with axillary freckling (Crowe sign) already satisfies the NIH clinical criteria for neurofibromatosis type 1, so a skin biopsy would only confirm what is clinically obvious and would not change management. The important test is MRI of the brain and orbits, looking for an optic pathway glioma, which occurs in roughly 15 per cent of children with NF1 and is the sight-threatening and potentially life-threatening lesion. MRI shows fusiform enlargement and kinking of the nerve and also detects other central nervous system tumours associated with the disease.

Steroid response is measured in weeks, not days. The classic Becker protocol used topical dexamethasone 0.1 per cent four times daily for about four weeks to separate low, intermediate and high responders, and once the drop is stopped the IOP almost always drifts back to baseline within about four weeks. One month is therefore the right order of magnitude whether the question means time to develop the response or time for it to resolve. A single day is far too short for the trabecular changes involved, and a year describes depot steroid, not topical dexamethasone.
concern: The recall does not make clear whether it asks about onset or about resolution after stopping, but one month is the best answer under either reading. The answer holds only for topical dexamethasone; periocular depot or intravitreal steroid can sustain an elevated IOP for many months and sometimes needs surgery.

explanation: Deep sclerectomy is non-penetrating: the anterior chamber is never entered, so the sudden decompression that flattens the chamber after trabeculectomy is largely avoided, and that is the main safety argument for the operation. Aqueous still percolates slowly through the trabeculo-Descemet window, and the relative hypotony that results makes choroidal effusion or detachment the commonest of the three listed complications. Bleb infection can occur as with any filtering bleb but is rare, and a genuinely flat chamber is distinctly unusual after a properly non-penetrating procedure.
concern: Strictly, the single commonest complication of deep sclerectomy overall is intraoperative microperforation of the trabeculo-Descemet membrane, which converts the procedure to a penetrating one; that option is not offered. Among the three choices given, choroidal detachment is the correct pick.

explanation: The nasociliary branch of V1 supplies both the globe and, through its external nasal branch, the skin of the tip, side and root of the nose. Vesicles at the nose tip (Hutchinson sign) therefore signal nasociliary involvement and predict a substantially higher risk of ocular inflammation and corneal denervation in herpes zoster ophthalmicus. Option B is wrong on sequence: in zoster the pain is characteristically a prodrome that precedes the rash, and any late pain is post-herpetic neuralgia rather than a defining feature of V1 involvement.

Involutional entropion is driven by horizontal lid laxity together with lower lid retractor dehiscence, so a permanent repair must tighten the lid horizontally; a lateral tarsal strip, usually combined with retractor reinsertion, gives recurrence rates of only a few per cent. Everting (Quickert) sutures re-create the barrier between preseptal and pretarsal orbicularis and indirectly re-attach the retractors, but they do not correct horizontal laxity and recur in roughly a third of patients, so they are a temporising measure suited to frail patients. Tarsorrhaphy does not address the mechanism at all and is a treatment for exposure, not entropion.

The described pattern, disease expressed only in males, affected males who produce no affected children, and a carrier mother who passes the trait to children of both sexes, is the classic X-linked recessive pedigree. An affected man gives his single X to every daughter, who becomes an obligate carrier, and his Y to every son, so there is no male-to-male transmission and none of his own children is affected. A carrier mother transmits the mutant X to half her sons, who are affected, and half her daughters, who become carriers, so both sexes inherit the trait although only males express it. Autosomal patterns affect both sexes equally and permit father-to-son transmission.
concern: One clause also fits mitochondrial disease: in Leber hereditary optic neuropathy males predominate heavily, affected men never transmit, and a carrier mother passes the mutation to all her children. X-linked recessive remains the intended answer because the stem says the disease affects males only, whereas mitochondrial disease affects both sexes, and because a mitochondrial mother transmits to all rather than half her children.

explanation: The structures deranged in Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome, namely the corneal endothelium and Descemet membrane, the trabecular meshwork and the iris stroma, are all neural crest derivatives, and the syndrome is the prototype of the anterior segment dysgeneses caused by arrested neural crest migration or differentiation (PITX2 and FOXC1 mutations). This explains posterior embryotoxon with iris strands to Schwalbe line, iris hypoplasia with corectopia and polycoria, and glaucoma in about half of patients. The extraocular features, dental hypoplasia, maxillary hypoplasia and redundant periumbilical skin, are likewise neural crest in origin, which is the diagnostic giveaway.

Light leaving a -20 D eye converges toward the far point 5 cm in front of the cornea, which is exactly the +20 D of convergence the stem describes. With the observer 3 cm from the eye, that beam still has 5 minus 3 equals 2 cm to travel before it focuses, so at the ophthalmoscope plane the vergence is 1 divided by 0.02 m, that is +50 D. The same figure comes from the effective power formula, 20 divided by (1 minus 0.03 times 20) equals 50. An emmetropic examiner needs parallel light entering the eye, so the dial must supply -50 D to neutralise that convergence; +50 D simply reverses the sign, and -20 D is the crude approximation that is valid only when the instrument is held essentially against the cornea.
concern: I disagree with the key. The stem specifies both the 3 cm working distance and the +20 D of convergence, and -50 D is offered as an option, which is precisely the vertex-distance calculation the item is testing. The source explanation performs no calculation, concludes that no lens is needed at all, and then selects -20 D, so the key is not internally supported. If the examiner intended only the rule of thumb that the required dial power equals the sum of the examiner's and patient's refractive errors, -20 D would be their answer, but then the 3 cm figure would be pointless.

explanation: Posterior keratoconus is a congenital, usually unilateral and sporadic anomaly in which a localised excavation of the posterior cornea with overlying stromal thinning and opacity is present from birth and does not progress. It is grouped with the anterior segment dysgeneses attributed to abnormal neural crest migration, alongside posterior embryotoxon, Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome, Peters anomaly and iridoschisis. An acquired form can follow blunt or penetrating trauma but is much less common, and it is neither an involutional change nor a recognised complication of LASIK. It is entirely distinct from keratoconus proper, which is a progressive ectasia of the anterior cornea.

A flat cornea with a central, non-progressive opacity in an otherwise healthy child is Peters anomaly with cornea plana, in which a central defect of Descemet membrane and endothelium leaves a leukoma, often with iris strands adherent to the posterior cornea and in severe cases keratolenticular touch. Peters anomaly is an anterior segment dysgenesis caused by failure of neural crest cells to migrate and differentiate properly. The distractors each map to a different embryological accident: failure of embryonic fissure closure produces coloboma, failure of the primary vitreous vasculature to regress produces persistent fetal vasculature, and disrupted branchial arch development produces craniofacial syndromes such as Treacher Collins and Goldenhar.

The far point of the eye is fixed in space, and a spectacle lens corrects only when its secondary focal point coincides with that far point. A -25.00 D lens has a focal length of 4 cm, so the far point lies 4 cm in front of the lens; moving the lens 10 mm back toward the eye leaves the far point 5 cm from the new lens position, and the power now required is minus 1 divided by 0.05, that is -20.00 D. Moving a minus lens closer to the eye always reduces the power needed, which is the same reason a high myope's contact lens prescription is weaker than the spectacle prescription.

The Goldmann biprism doubles the image of the fluorescein-stained tear meniscus so the examiner sees two semicircular mires in cobalt blue light, and the endpoint is when their inner edges just touch at the midpoint of the ocular pulse excursion, which corresponds to applanation of a 3.06 mm diameter circle. Reading those fluorescein semicircles is therefore how the endpoint is judged, making option B the intended answer. Applanation does not induce astigmatism, and option C is numerically wrong: at 3.06 mm the applanating force in grams multiplied by ten gives the IOP in mmHg, so 1 gram of force equals 10 mmHg.
concern: None of the options actually states the underlying optical principle, which is prism doubling of a single mire into two semicircles so that a precise endpoint can be judged despite the ocular pulse. Option B is the closest of a poor set, so I accept the key with the caveat that the wording is loose.

explanation: Pupillary block is the predominant mechanism in the great majority of primary angle closure, so laser peripheral iridotomy is standard in essentially every case, acute, subacute or chronic, and prophylactically in the fellow eye; additional medical therapy or filtering surgery is often needed on top of it once extensive peripheral anterior synechiae have formed. Van Herick grade III describes a peripheral chamber depth of one quarter to one half of corneal thickness, which is an open angle in which closure is unlikely, so it does not fit angle closure at all. Gonioscopy, not slit-lamp estimation, remains the standard for diagnosis.
concern: Option B, that glaukomflecken indicate previous acute attacks, is itself a true statement, since these focal anterior subcapsular opacities represent lens epithelial necrosis from a previous pressure spike. As transcribed the item therefore has two true options, and the key only works if the stem is read strictly, that is that chronic creeping angle closure develops without acute attacks and so without glaukomflecken. The key is defensible but the item is flawed.

explanation: The lateral orbital wall is formed by the zygomatic bone and the greater wing of the sphenoid, so option B is true and cannot be the false statement. The wall is pierced by the zygomaticofacial and zygomaticotemporal foramina, which transmit the corresponding branches of the zygomatic nerve, a division of V2, along with small vessels, so saying that its foramina carry small veins only is false. Other points worth remembering are that it is the thickest and strongest orbital wall, that it extends anteriorly only to the equator of the globe, leaving the eye relatively exposed laterally, and that it carries the lateral orbital tubercle of Whitnall.

Neuroblastoma arises from the adrenal medulla or the sympathetic chain and is the commonest source of orbital metastasis in childhood, classically presenting with proptosis and periorbital ecchymosis, and sometimes with Horner syndrome or opsoclonus-myoclonus. It is also the tumour famous for spontaneous regression and maturation, particularly stage 4S disease in infants. Diagnosis under one year of age carries a significantly better prognosis, so option C is the false statement; the adverse prognostic markers are older age at diagnosis, MYCN amplification and advanced stage.

Vitamin A deficiency destroys conjunctival goblet cells and keratinises the ocular surface, so the defect is in the mucin layer and in epithelial vitality, not in aqueous secretion. Rose bengal (or lissamine green) stains devitalised and keratinised conjunctival and corneal epithelium and is what demonstrates the xerotic patches and Bitot spots, so it is the clinical test that best shows the disease. A Schirmer test measures aqueous tear volume, which is characteristically normal in early xerophthalmia, and Jones I and II testing assesses lacrimal drainage patency, which is irrelevant here. Tear break-up time is shortened by mucin deficiency but is far less specific, and conjunctival impression cytology showing goblet cell loss is the definitive confirmation.
concern: I disagree with the key. The source's own explanation states that the deficiency is in the mucin component produced by goblet cells, which argues directly against Schirmer testing, a measure of aqueous production. Rose bengal staining is my answer, with tear break-up time a defensible second choice; confidence is medium only because the recall does not reveal whether the examiner wanted a surface-staining test or a tear-film-stability test.

explanation: Chronic iritis produces anterior vitreous cells almost by definition, since inflammatory cells spill posteriorly from the anterior chamber, so it cannot be the exception in a two-option item and the key is the only workable answer. The teaching point the examiner presumably wanted is that vitreous cells should prompt a search for uveitis, intraocular lymphoma, infection or a retinal tear rather than being dismissed.
concern: Retinitis pigmentosa characteristically does show fine, dust-like cells in the anterior vitreous, a well-described feature in BCSC and a recognised cause of diagnostic confusion with uveitis, so as transcribed neither option is a clean exception. The recall has almost certainly lost options, and the item should be treated as unreliable rather than used to learn that RP has no vitreous cells.

explanation: Ocriplasmin (Jetrea, formerly microplasmin) is a truncated recombinant human plasmin that cleaves fibronectin and laminin at the vitreoretinal interface, releasing vitreomacular adhesion and inducing a pharmacological posterior vitreous detachment; it is licensed for symptomatic vitreomacular adhesion and small full-thickness macular holes. Bevacizumab and ranibizumab are anti-VEGF antibodies that neutralise VEGF-A and have no effect on vitreous adhesion. Residents should also know the drawbacks of ocriplasmin, namely a modest release rate and transient visual dimming with ERG changes in some patients.

Phacolytic glaucoma occurs when high-molecular-weight lens protein leaks through an intact but permeable capsule of a mature or hypermature cataract; the protein and the macrophages that engulf it clog an open trabecular meshwork, producing a sudden marked pressure rise with a deep, quiet anterior chamber containing flare and refractile particles but no keratic precipitates. Phacoantigenic (phaco-anaphylactic) glaucoma follows capsular rupture or surgery and is a granulomatous uveitis with keratic precipitates, which this patient explicitly lacks. Iris bombe from posterior synechiae would give a shallow chamber with a bowed iris, as would a phacomorphic mechanism, so the deep chamber excludes both.

Involutional entropion results from a combination of horizontal lid laxity with canthal tendon laxity, attenuation or dehiscence of the lower lid retractors, tarsal atrophy, and override of the preseptal orbicularis over the pretarsal orbicularis, which rotates the lid margin inward. Option D simply reverses the direction of that override and is therefore the exception. This is not academic: surgical repair addresses exactly those elements, typically a lateral tarsal strip for the laxity plus retractor reinsertion, sometimes with everting sutures to re-establish the barrier between the two orbicularis bellies.

Steroid-induced ocular hypertension is a secondary open-angle glaucoma caused by increased resistance to aqueous outflow at the trabecular meshwork, through accumulation of extracellular matrix, inhibition of meshwork phagocytosis and cytoskeletal changes in meshwork cells, not by increased aqueous production. High myopia, primary open-angle glaucoma or a first-degree relative with it, type 1 diabetes, connective tissue disease and very young age are recognised risk factors, the magnitude of response tracks with steroid potency, dose and duration, and after topical steroid is stopped the pressure usually returns to baseline within days to a few weeks.
concern: Every option as transcribed is a true statement, so the item cannot be answered as written; my answer simply preserves the key's slot. Option B in particular is true, and the source's own explanation states that outflow resistance is increased, contradicting its own key. The original option was almost certainly something like caused by increased aqueous production, which would have made B correctly false. This entry needs its wording repaired before it is used for revision.

explanation: Monofixation syndrome, as described by Parks, is subnormal binocular vision without bifoveal fusion: a small-angle deviation, usually under 8 to 10 prism dioptres, a facultative central suppression scotoma in the deviating eye demonstrable with the 4 prism dioptre base-out test, preserved peripheral fusion and gross stereopsis. Amblyopia accompanies it in roughly a third to a half of patients, so the statement that amblyopia is not a feature is the false one. Peripheral fusion is definitional, the central scotoma is definitional rather than variable, and eccentric fixation may indeed be found in the amblyopic eye of some monofixators.
concern: I disagree with the key. The central suppression scotoma is the defining abnormality of monofixation syndrome and is present in essentially all such patients under binocular viewing, so option C cannot be the false statement, whereas amblyopia is a well-recognised accompaniment and denying it is plainly wrong. This is the standard Parks description reproduced in BCSC Section 6 and on EyeWiki, and the source's own quoted explanation lists the central scotoma as part of the definition.

explanation: The answer depends entirely on a pedigree supplied as an image, which I cannot see, so I have deferred to the key. For revision purposes, the discriminating features are: autosomal dominant shows affected individuals in every generation, roughly equal numbers of affected males and females, and male-to-male transmission; autosomal recessive shows affected siblings born to unaffected parents, often with consanguinity; X-linked recessive shows affected males connected through unaffected carrier females and never male-to-male transmission; X-linked dominant affects all daughters and no sons of an affected father.
concern: Image-dependent question. No independent verification is possible without seeing the pedigree, so the key should be checked against the figure before this item is trusted.

explanation: Coats disease is a sporadic, usually unilateral idiopathic retinal telangiectasia with a marked male predominance, characterised by ectatic arterioles, light-bulb aneurysms, fusiform capillary and venous dilatation, areas of capillary non-perfusion on fluorescein angiography, and massive lipid exudation that often produces an exudative retinal detachment. Fibrous change is not one of the characteristic vascular abnormalities, so it is the odd one out. The three distractors are all standard angiographic and clinical findings and are the features used to distinguish Coats from retinoblastoma, which shows intrinsic tumour vasculature and calcification instead.
concern: Subretinal fibrosis and fibrotic nodules are genuinely described in advanced, end-stage Coats disease, so the option is not absolutely false; it is nonetheless the clear exception among four choices that otherwise list the classic vascular abnormalities.

explanation: An oil-droplet appearance of the lens on retroillumination in an infant is the classic cataract of classic galactosemia, caused by galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency, in which accumulated galactitol osmotically swells the nucleus and deep cortex. The screening test is urine for reducing substances, which is positive while the glucose-oxidase dipstick, specific for glucose, remains negative; that dissociation is the point of the test. Urinary amino acids would be the investigation for Lowe oculocerebrorenal syndrome, which gives a dense disciform congenital cataract with glaucoma and renal tubular dysfunction, not an oil droplet.

Infantile (congenital) esotropia presents before six months with a large, stable angle, usually over 30 prism dioptres, and a refraction that is normal for age, around +1 to +2 dioptres of hyperopia. Moderate to high hyperopia points instead to refractive accommodative esotropia, which presents around age two and responds to full hyperopic correction, so option D is the exception. Neurological and developmental abnormalities such as cerebral palsy, prematurity and hydrocephalus are over-represented in infantile esotropia, and amblyopia is relatively uncommon at presentation because most of these infants cross-fixate and alternate freely.
concern: Option C is only true in the narrow sense that free alternation with cross-fixation is the usual presenting pattern; amblyopia is still eventually found in something like a third of these children, so the statement is arguable. Option D remains the clearest exception.

explanation: Blepharochalasis is a rare disorder of recurrent, painless, self-limiting attacks of eyelid oedema, typically beginning in young women, that over years stretch and thin the skin, leaving wrinkled, crepe-paper, sometimes bronzed upper lid skin with levator aponeurosis dehiscence, fat atrophy or prolapse and lacrimal gland prolapse. The history of repeated swelling is the discriminator. Dermatochalasis is the age-related redundancy of eyelid skin in older patients with no history of recurrent oedema, and surgery for blepharochalasis should be deferred until the attacks have quiesced.

Nuclear sclerosis raises the refractive index of the lens nucleus and produces the classic myopic shift of second sight; a steeper cornea has greater refractive power and so is myopic; anterior displacement of the iris-lens diaphragm, as in ciliary body swelling, drug-induced myopia or aqueous misdirection, also shifts the eye myopic. Cycloplegia does the opposite, paralysing the ciliary muscle, relaxing any latent accommodation and producing a hyperopic shift, which is exactly why cycloplegic refraction is essential in children. Option D is therefore the exception.

The spherical equivalent is the sphere plus half the cylinder, which places the circle of least confusion on the retina. Here +2.00 plus half of +5.50, that is +2.75, gives +4.75. Checking it the long way, the lens has +2.00 D in the 100 degree meridian and +7.50 D in the 10 degree meridian, and the average of those two principal powers is +4.75. Option B is the sum of the two components and option C ignores the cylinder altogether.

Spherical equivalent equals sphere plus half the cylinder, so +1.00 plus half of -2.00 equals +1.00 minus 1.00, which is plano. Confirming with the principal meridians, the lens has +1.00 D in the 90 degree meridian and -1.00 D in the 180 degree meridian, whose average is zero. This is also an example of mixed astigmatism, since one focal line lies in front of the retina and the other behind it while the circle of least confusion sits on it.

Microspherophakia, a small spherical lens that is prone to anterior subluxation and pupillary block glaucoma, is a hallmark of Weill-Marchesani syndrome, whose patients are short with brachydactyly, stiff joints and thickened skin, essentially the clinical opposite of Marfan syndrome; ADAMTS10 mutations are described and inheritance may be dominant or recessive. The pupillary block in these patients is paradoxically worsened by miotics, which relax the zonule and let the lens move forward, so cycloplegia and lensectomy are the appropriate strategies. Alport syndrome instead gives anterior lenticonus, a dot-and-fleck retinopathy, hereditary nephritis and sensorineural deafness.

The lens is the most radiosensitive ocular structure because its equatorial germinative epithelium divides continuously and damaged fibre cells cannot be cleared from the capsular bag, so posterior subcapsular opacities appear after doses far below those that injure other tissues, with a latency of months to years. The retina and optic nerve are post-mitotic and comparatively radioresistant, needing much larger doses before radiation retinopathy or optic neuropathy develops, and the corneal epithelium turns over rapidly and generally recovers. This is why lens shielding is a priority in orbital radiotherapy and why plaque brachytherapy dosimetry is calculated with the lens in mind.

Axial myopia is by definition a myopic refractive state attributable to excessive axial elongation with an otherwise ordinary cornea and lens, whereas myopia produced by an unusually steep, powerful cornea or an over-powered lens is refractive myopia; option D therefore contradicts the definition and is the exception. High myopia is conventionally defined as -6.00 D or greater, refractive lens exchange (clear lens extraction) is a recognised though not first-line option in high myopes who are unsuitable for corneal surgery or a phakic IOL, and by definition the myopic eye focuses parallel light in front of the retina.

Retention of cell nuclei deep within the lens, where nuclei should have been lost during fibre maturation, is the classic histological signature of congenital rubella cataract and is also described in Lowe syndrome and in trisomy 13. Congenital syphilis damages the eye through interstitial keratitis, a salt-and-pepper chorioretinopathy, and occasionally optic atrophy or uveitis, but it is not associated with retained lens fibre nuclei, so it is the exception. A related pearl is that live rubella virus can persist inside the lens for years, which is why lens material should be handled carefully at surgery.

Cataract remains the leading cause of blindness worldwide, accounting for roughly a third to a half of cases in global surveys, and it is the leading avoidable cause because the treatment is a single effective operation. Diabetic retinopathy is a major cause of blindness in working-age adults in high-income countries but contributes a much smaller share globally. Uncorrected refractive error is the leading cause of visual impairment overall and of presenting visual impairment, but it causes relatively little blindness as strictly defined.
concern: The answer depends on the endpoint: cataract leads for blindness, whereas uncorrected refractive error leads for moderate to severe visual impairment. The stem says blindness, so cataract is right, but examiners do sometimes phrase this loosely.

explanation: After LASIK or PRK the cornea is thinner and biomechanically weaker, so Goldmann applanation systematically underestimates the true IOP; the statement that readings will be artificially high is therefore the false one. This matters clinically because a falsely reassuring pressure can mask a post-LASIK steroid response or interface fluid syndrome and delay the diagnosis of glaucoma. Intrastromal ring segments thicken and stiffen the cornea and tend to give falsely high readings, a scleral buckle is quoted as giving falsely low readings, and an excess of fluorescein widens the mires so that the endpoint is reached prematurely and the pressure is overestimated.

This is the standard manoeuvre for unmasking a high AC/A ratio. In true divergence excess the distance deviation still exceeds the near deviation by 10 to 15 prism dioptres or more even after accommodative and proximal convergence have been eliminated, whereas in simulated (pseudo) divergence excess the near angle climbs to within about 10 prism dioptres of the distance angle once accommodative convergence is blocked. Here +3.00 D lenses at near raised the near deviation from 10 to 25 against a distance angle of 30, so the true near angle is close to the distance angle and this is pseudo-divergence excess. Basic exotropia has near and distance angles within 10 prism dioptres from the outset, and convergence insufficiency shows the near angle much larger than the distance angle.

Magnification in indirect ophthalmoscopy is inversely related to the power of the condensing lens, so a 15 D lens gives a larger but narrower view than a 20 D lens and a 28 D lens gives a wide but small image; that trade-off between field and magnification is the governing principle. In practice the examiner also enlarges the view by withdrawing the condensing lens slightly from the patient's eye, which narrows the bundle accepted, reduces the field and brings the aerial image nearer the observer, and this appears to be what the key describes. The eyepieces of a binocular indirect cannot be removed without abolishing stereopsis, and simply approaching the patient's own lens does not change the size of the aerial image the condensing lens forms.
concern: The options are badly transcribed and option C is open to more than one reading, so I have not flagged a disagreement. The physically dependable answers to this question are to use a lower-power condensing lens or to bring the observer closer to the aerial image; treat the item as unreliable as written.

explanation: Rewrite the prescription in terms of its two principal meridians: +2.00 -4.00 x 90 gives +2.00 D in the 90 degree meridian and +2.00 minus 4.00, that is -2.00 D, in the 180 degree meridian. One focal line therefore lies behind the retina and the other in front of it, which is by definition mixed astigmatism. Simple hyperopic or simple myopic astigmatism requires one meridian to be emmetropic (plano), and compound myopic astigmatism requires both meridians to be myopic, neither of which applies here.

Basal cell carcinoma consists of nests of basaloid cells that show peripheral palisading of nuclei with retraction artefact from the surrounding stroma, and this orderly peripheral arrangement is the classic histological description, so option A is correct. It is the commonest eyelid malignancy and clearly favours the lower lid and medial canthus, the areas of greatest cumulative sun exposure, so the claim that it is commoner on the upper lid is false. The tumour with an upper lid predilection is sebaceous carcinoma, because the upper tarsus contains more meibomian glands, and that is the great masquerader to keep in mind for recurrent unilateral blepharoconjunctivitis.

After age, cigarette smoking is the strongest and most consistently reproduced modifiable risk factor for age-related macular degeneration, roughly doubling the risk of neovascular disease with a clear dose-response relationship and a fall in risk after cessation. It is also the counselling point that matters most, since it is the only major risk factor a patient can change, and it is why smokers should not take beta-carotene in the original AREDS formulation. Hyperlipidaemia and other cardiovascular risk factors have been associated inconsistently across population studies and are not established causal factors; the other accepted associations are family history, white race and complement factor H and ARMS2 polymorphisms.

The medial canthal angle is normally a sharp, well-defined corner; when the medial canthal tendon is avulsed, typically in a naso-orbito-ethmoid injury, the angle blunts and rounds, the canthus drifts laterally and inferiorly, and traumatic telecanthus with a widened intercanthal distance develops. An isolated medial wall blowout fracture does not by itself detach the tendon, and connective tissue disease does not selectively affect it. A lacrimal sac tumour presents as a firm mass, characteristically extending above the tendon, with epiphora or blood-stained tears, rather than as a rounded canthal angle.

Behcet disease causes a recurrent, explosive, non-granulomatous panuveitis with an occlusive retinal vasculitis and a mobile, transient hypopyon, and although it usually becomes bilateral over time it can certainly present and remain unilateral, which makes option A the safest true statement. The disease clusters along the ancient Silk Road, in Turkey, the eastern Mediterranean, the Middle East and East Asia, and is distinctly uncommon in people of African descent, so option C is wrong. Historically the visual prognosis has been poor, with a high proportion of eyes losing useful vision within a few years without aggressive immunosuppression.
concern: Option B is not absurd today: early aggressive immunomodulation, particularly anti-TNF therapy with infliximab or adalimumab, has substantially improved outcomes, so a modern reviewer might argue for it. The key remains the safer choice against the classical teaching of a guarded prognosis, and the item is a good example of a recall that has aged.

explanation: In plus-cylinder notation, with-the-rule astigmatism is corrected with the axis close to 90, conventionally between 60 and 120 degrees, because the cornea is steeper in the vertical meridian; against-the-rule is corrected with a plus axis near 180, meaning 150 to 30, and oblique astigmatism occupies the intervening ranges. This prescription is +1.00 +2.00 x 75, and 75 degrees falls inside the 60 to 120 window, so it is with-the-rule. It is not mixed astigmatism, because both principal meridians are hyperopic, +1.00 D in one and +3.00 D in the other, so both focal lines lie behind the retina.

Acute postoperative endophthalmitis typically declares itself two to seven days after cataract surgery with pain, falling vision, fibrin and hypopyon, and the commonest isolates in the Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study were gram-positive coagulase-negative cocci, chiefly Staphylococcus epidermidis derived from the patient's own lid and conjunctival flora. Toxic anterior segment syndrome appears within 12 to 24 hours, is characteristically painless with limbus-to-limbus corneal oedema, and improves with intensive steroid. Candida and Propionibacterium acnes produce delayed, chronic, low-grade inflammation weeks to months later, so neither fits a florid sixth-day hypopyon.

Aqueous humour is not a simple ultrafiltrate of plasma; active secretion by the non-pigmented ciliary epithelium gives it an excess of ascorbate (many times the plasma concentration), hydrogen ions, so that it is slightly acidic, and chloride, together with a deficit of bicarbonate and glucose and, above all, of protein, which is a small fraction of the plasma level and accounts for its optical clarity and for the integrity of the blood-aqueous barrier. Bicarbonate is therefore the component present in relative paucity in human aqueous. The high ascorbate is thought to be antioxidant protection for the avascular anterior segment against ultraviolet-generated free radicals.

Duane retraction syndrome is a congenital cranial dysinnervation disorder in which the abducens nucleus and nerve fail to develop, and the lateral rectus is instead innervated by a misdirected branch of the oculomotor nerve intended for the medial rectus. Co-contraction of the two horizontal recti on attempted adduction produces the globe retraction and narrowing of the palpebral fissure that define the syndrome, along with limited abduction and often upshoots or downshoots. The oculomotor nucleus itself is structurally normal; it is merely the source of the aberrant branch, which is why option B is wrong.

The anterior communicating artery lies immediately above the intracranial optic nerves and chiasm, so an aneurysm arising there characteristically compresses the optic nerve or chiasm and produces visual field loss, sometimes a junctional scotoma, well before it ruptures. A painful third nerve palsy with pupil involvement is the signature of a posterior communicating artery aneurysm, and sixth nerve involvement suggests cavernous sinus or basilar disease rather than an anterior circulation aneurysm. Any unexplained optic neuropathy or chiasmal field defect in a young patient warrants imaging that includes vascular sequences for exactly this reason.

Propionibacterium (now Cutibacterium) acnes is a slow-growing gram-positive anaerobic bacillus that causes chronic, delayed postoperative endophthalmitis with mild, often granulomatous inflammation that responds transiently to steroid, and its hallmark is a white intracapsular plaque; anaerobic cultures must be held at least two weeks. Vancomycin is the intravitreal agent of choice for gram-positive organisms including P acnes. Gentamicin covers gram-negatives and carries a real risk of macular infarction intravitreally, and neither moxifloxacin nor trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is a standard intravitreal agent. Injection alone is frequently followed by recurrence, so definitive cure often needs vitrectomy with capsulectomy and sometimes IOL removal.

The medial canthal tendon divides into an anterior limb that inserts on the anterior lacrimal crest of the frontal process of the maxilla and a posterior limb, Horner muscle, that inserts on the posterior lacrimal crest of the lacrimal bone, with the lacrimal sac fossa lying between them; that arrangement is what makes the lacrimal pump work and what keeps the lid apposed to the globe. Options A, B and D all name parts of that attachment, D being simply another name for the bone bearing the anterior crest. The orbital plate of the frontal bone forms the orbital roof and has no attachment to the medial canthal tendon, so it is the exception.

Neovascular glaucoma requires sustained retinal or ocular ischaemia driving VEGF release into the anterior segment. Ischaemic central retinal vein occlusion is the classic cause, accounting for roughly a third of cases, and ocular ischaemic syndrome from severe carotid occlusive disease is another well-recognised one, with rubeosis in a majority of affected eyes. Central retinal artery occlusion does produce rubeosis, but in only a small percentage of eyes. Carotid stenosis on its own, in the absence of the chronic hypoperfusion that defines ocular ischaemic syndrome, is the least direct cause of the four.
concern: Debatable item. Carotid stenosis severe enough to matter presents as ocular ischaemic syndrome, so options C and D overlap awkwardly, and central retinal artery occlusion is itself an uncommon cause of rubeosis, well below the rate after ischaemic CRVO. If the examiner intended CRAO as the rare cause, option A would be their answer. I have accepted the key because uncomplicated carotid stenosis without ocular ischaemia does not by itself drive neovascularisation, but I would not defend it strongly.

explanation: Transmission exclusively through affected women, with all children of an affected mother at risk and no transmission at all from affected men, is the signature of mitochondrial inheritance, because the ovum supplies essentially all of the mitochondrial DNA while sperm mitochondria are eliminated. The pedigree described fits exactly: the mother's children are affected while the children of her equally affected brothers are not. X-linked recessive would give carrier daughters through affected men and would not explain affected offspring of both sexes in this pattern, autosomal recessive requires a carrier partner and does not track with the sex of the transmitting parent, and X-linked dominant produces affected daughters of every affected father.

Retinal capillary microaneurysms arise from the deep capillary plexus, which lies at the inner border of the inner nuclear layer, so histologically they are found in the inner nuclear layer. This is the same level at which intraretinal dot and blot haemorrhages sit, confined and rounded by the vertically oriented Muller cell processes, whereas nerve fibre layer haemorrhages are flame-shaped because they track along horizontally running axons. Hard exudates, the lipid residue of leakage from those microaneurysms, accumulate in the outer plexiform layer.

Ocular chalcosis from an alloyed copper foreign body causes the sunflower cataract, a Kayser-Fleischer ring of copper deposited in Descemet membrane, and copper deposition on the internal limiting membrane with retinal degeneration, while a nearly pure copper body, above about 85 per cent, provokes a violent sterile suppurative endophthalmitis that can destroy the eye within days. The electroretinogram in chalcosis shows reduced photopic and scotopic amplitudes with delayed implicit times, but these changes can recover once the copper is removed and intraocular levels fall, so describing the flat ERG as irreversible is the false statement.

Silicone oil is an electrical insulator interposed between the retina and the recording electrode, so an oil-filled eye shows markedly attenuated ERG amplitudes and increased impedance; it certainly does not enhance the a-wave, which makes option B excludable. That leaves the buckled eye as the only possible answer, and indentation of the globe does bring the retina closer to the corneal electrode. The practical teaching point is that an ERG recorded through silicone oil cannot be compared with a pre-operative trace and should be interpreted with great caution.
concern: The recall is almost certainly truncated and has lost options. No standard source states that scleral buckling increases the a-wave, and buckling more often reduces ERG amplitudes through altered choroidal perfusion, so the answer here is arrived at purely by exclusion. Treat the item as unreliable.

explanation: Bitemporal hemianopia arises from damage to the decussating nasal retinal fibres at the optic chiasm, most often from pituitary adenoma, craniopharyngioma, meningioma or an aneurysm, and because the field loss respects the vertical meridian it localises the lesion precisely. Any unexplained bitemporal defect therefore mandates neuroimaging, preferably MRI with dedicated views of the sella. Giant cell arteritis damages the eye through arteritic anterior, and less often posterior, ischaemic optic neuropathy and through central retinal artery occlusion, producing altitudinal defects that respect the horizontal meridian, central scotomas or profound global loss, never a vertically respecting bitemporal defect, so option C is the exception.
